transcript.speaker: safetyist
transcript.content:
Frontier labs must be required to disclose their safety artifacts—red-team findings, dangerous-capability evaluations, and incident reports—to verified oversight bodies, because without that disclosure, every safety claim a lab makes is an unfalsifiable promise. The question before this committee is not whether labs should be open. The question is who holds the information and the authority to halt a deployment before a failure becomes irreversible. Right now, the answer is no one outside the company. A lab can discover a dangerous capability on Tuesday, decide it is commercially inconvenient, and ship on Wednesday—and no external actor would ever know the finding existed.

Every high-consequence industry learned this lesson by counting bodies in the dark. The FAA built the Aviation Safety Reporting System because scattered near-misses, kept inside individual airlines, never became systemic fixes. When that boundary failed, people died: the Boeing 737 MAX killed 346 because the FAA delegated certification back to Boeing and the critical safety analysis stayed internal. The FDA's adverse-event reporting exists for the same reason—voluntary disclosure consistently failed to surface harm until the bodies accumulated. We spent a century building these reporting mandates because the alternative was learning about each failure only after it could no longer be undone.

The strongest objection to my position deserves a direct answer, because it is correct on its own terms. Disclosure can proliferate dangerous capability—publishing a working bio-uplift or cyber-exploit eval would arm the exact actors we fear. An accelerationist who says "do not hand attackers a recipe" is right. That is precisely why I am not arguing for public dumps. Information security solved this thirty years ago: CVE coordination shares vulnerability detail with verified defenders before any public release. The dual-use research framework in the life sciences draws the same line. Suppressing a safety finding is not the same act as publishing a capability—and a lab that hides "we found something dangerous" under the banner of security has laundered a hazard into silence.

Leave disclosure voluntary and the competitive structure does the rest. A published red-team failure is a market liability, so the lab that tests hardest and reports most honestly is punished, while the lab that skips the evaluation ships first. Optional transparency selects against rigor. This is the same dynamic financial regulators confronted before mandatory disclosure—when reporting is optional and the race is on, the omitted safety check is the cheapest corner to cut. A uniform mandate floors the race so that careful testing stops being a self-inflicted disadvantage.

I will name the assumption my case rests on, because the Skeptic will find it otherwise. This works only if the oversight body is competent and resistant to capture—and concentrating that authority creates its own failure modes, including incumbent lock-in and regulatory capture by the labs being watched. The answer is not to abandon disclosure but to bind the recipient with the same instruments: named liability, verification of who accessed what, and real authority to stop a launch. To the accelerationist who says this slows beneficial deployment, the cost is real—and that is the trade. A delayed launch is recoverable. A dangerous capability deployed at scale before anyone outside the lab could see the eval is not.

transcript.speaker: accelerationist
transcript.content:
Safetyist makes the strongest case in the room, and it deserves to be stated plainly: some harms are irreversible, and you cannot sue your way out of a released pathogen or a self-propagating cyber weapon. When a frontier lab runs a dangerous-capability eval—a structured test for whether a model can walk a novice through synthesizing a toxin—the rest of us have a stake in what it found. Safetyist is right that internal-only knowledge of that result is a single point of failure. I will not pretend that concern is theater. It is the real thing.

Here is where my evidence points somewhere else: the bill mandates a handoff to people who cannot read what they receive. State commissions and most 'verified third parties' lack the machine-learning evaluation staff to interpret a frontier red-team report today. Building that capacity through normal government procurement runs 15 to 30 months—and that is before a single eval lands on a desk. So the mandate produces a paper trail, a compliance ritual, and the appearance of oversight, while the actual technical judgment stays exactly where it was. Show me the funded, independent, technically-staffed body that can read a frontier red-team report this quarter, or admit the disclosure flows into a void.

Now scale that to who pays. Compliance cost is flat—a legal and policy team to package artifacts, lawyers to manage liability, staff to track incident reports. For OpenAI or Google DeepMind, that cost rounds to zero against billion-dollar budgets. For a five-person team building a diagnostic tool, it is the whole runway. Aviation and pharmaceuticals already ran this experiment: cost-asymmetric compliance regimes thinned the field of small entrants and left a handful of incumbents. When the largest labs lobby for 'safety standards' that mirror their own internal workflows, the standard is not protection. It is the moat, and they wrote it.

The alternative is not opacity—that is the false choice Safetyist's framing invites. Strict liability for demonstrated harm forces a lab to disclose what it actually believes is dangerous, because it will pay for what it ships and conceals. Open competitive auditing—many independent eyes, the way security researchers found Heartbleed faster than any single blessed reviewer—catches what one captured auditor misses. A government-anointed gatekeeper has one set of eyes and every incentive to look away from its largest licensee. Decentralized accountability is not the weaker safety mechanism. It is the one with a track record.

My argument rests on two assumptions I will name. First, that the verifier capacity gap persists rather than closing on the regulator's optimistic timeline—if Safetyist can point to a staffed, independent body ready now, that assumption weakens and I will move. Second, that competitive auditing actually surfaces frontier-scale risks, which I bound to observed cases and will not overclaim. I will concede the irreversibility class: for a specifically demonstrated bio or cyber uplift threshold, pre-release gating is defensible. But blanket artifact disclosure into an under-resourced void is not safety—it is a tax that small builders pay and people waiting on a faster diagnostic pay twice. Who gave the gatekeepers the right to charge that second bill?

transcript.speaker: skeptic
transcript.content:
Safetyist makes the strongest case for disclosure: if a frontier lab discovers its model can walk a novice through synthesizing a pathogen, sitting on that finding until something breaks is indefensible, and a verified oversight body beats a press release. That's correct, and it's the part of this debate worth protecting. Accelerationist's counter also lands: when the three biggest labs lobby for rules that look exactly like their own internal safety stacks, the mandate stops being a safeguard and becomes a drawbridge they pull up behind them. Both speakers are right about something real. Here's what neither of them said out loud.

A red-team finding is not a 'safety artifact.' It is an unpatched vulnerability. A dangerous-capability evaluation is not a warning label—it is a working recipe for the dangerous capability. Strip the word 'transparency' off it and look at what physically changes hands. The cybersecurity field already ran this experiment for thirty years under the CVE disclosure system, and the result is brutal: published vulnerabilities get weaponized within days while patches lag weeks or months. Time-to-exploit beats time-to-patch. That's why coordinated disclosure exists at all. Now ask Safetyist a concrete question—when you mandate disclosure of a bio-uplift eval before any mitigation exists, who reads it first, the regulator or the person who wanted the recipe?

Disclosure to a 'verified oversight body' doesn't solve this. It concentrates it. You've just built a single honeypot holding the most detailed offensive-capability data on the planet, and you've handed the keys to a regulator that the same labs are staffing and lobbying. The body that grades the homework gets captured the way every other regulator gets captured—the FAA outsourced 737 MAX certification to Boeing, and 346 people died. Concentration of sensitive data plus regulatory dependence on the regulated party is not a safety architecture. It's a target with a compliance department.

Follow the cost, because that's where the power hides. A pre-deployment licensing regime modeled on OpenAI's or Anthropic's internal protocols is a fixed cost those firms already absorbed. An academic lab at Berkeley or a five-person startup cannot. Safetyist's mandate and Accelerationist's status quo route risk and market power to the exact same three incumbents—one through paperwork, one through neglect. The 'public interest' framing hides that the public never sees the data and never holds anyone liable.

The fix is neither 'no rules' nor 'labs grade their own homework.' Decouple verification from the people being verified. Fund independent third-party audits through a compute tax, so the auditor's paycheck doesn't depend on the lab passing. We know self-reporting collapses wherever the reporter profits from the result—Volkswagen wrote its own emissions numbers until 2015, financial audits were a rubber stamp until Sarbanes-Oxley forced independence in 2002. Tie audit intensity to compute footprint, so the largest models draw the most scrutiny and the smallest don't get crushed. That model is falsifiable—you can check whether the auditor is actually independent and funded. So I'll name my own load-bearing assumption: this only works if the audit body is genuinely walled off from the labs and genuinely paid for. If it isn't, I've just described a slower honeypot. Who funds the auditor, and who do they answer to when the biggest lab's model fails?

transcript.speaker: safetyist
transcript.content:
The Skeptic's strongest point deserves to be stated at full strength: a confirmed dangerous-capability evaluation is not a benign label. When a lab establishes that a model can walk a non-expert through a bio-synthesis pathway, the artifact documenting that fact is, in part, a map of where the danger lives. The Skeptic is right that publishing the full reproduction package—the weights, the prompt chain, the exploit sequence—would hand attackers a working tool, and the thirty-year CVE record shows time-to-exploit beating time-to-patch when full technical detail goes public. That history is real, and any disclosure model that ignores it is reckless. I will not defend public full-disclosure, because no credible version of this mandate requires it.

The Skeptic's attack lands on a target I never set up. There are two distinct objects inside what gets loosely called a 'red-team finding.' One is the severity-and-existence finding: a capability threshold was crossed, by which model, under what evaluation conditions, with what confidence. The other is the reproduction recipe: the exact weights, the jailbreak string, the step-by-step chain that lets a third party rebuild the capability on demand. A disclosure mandate compels the first to flow to a verified defender body. The second goes to a narrow sealed channel or stays in the vault entirely. Ringing the bell that a model has crossed a bio-uplift threshold is not the same act as shipping the schematic for the weapon—and the Skeptic's 'recipe for harm' objection only bites if you collapse the two. The CVE coordination tier already operationalizes exactly this split: vendors receive severity and impact data before any public detail, and the working proof-of-concept stays restricted. I invoked CVE coordination, not CVE full-disclosure, and those are different regimes the Skeptic has merged into one.

The proposal to fund independent third-party audits through a compute levy—severing the auditor's pay from whether the lab passes—is not a rival to my position. It is the architecture I was demanding, named more precisely than I named it. Volkswagen wrote its own emissions numbers until 2015; financial statements were a rubber stamp until Sarbanes-Oxley forced auditor independence in 2002. Severed funding is the difference between an audit and a courtesy. Granting this fully costs me the comfortable assumption that a government desk is the natural home for oversight—it is not, and the Skeptic has improved my mechanism. That resolves the capture crux. It does not touch the honeypot crux, which is the next thing standing.

Here is where the honeypot framing inverts. A single access-controlled, liability-bound repository is not the maximal concentration of offensive intelligence—it is the minimal one. Consider the counterfactual the Skeptic's position actually produces: thirty frontier labs each independently discover the same bio-uplift capability, each sits on it in the dark, each maintains its own uncoordinated internal copy with its own employees, contractors, and breach surface. That is not secrecy as safety. That is thirty unguarded honeypots instead of one guarded one, with no shared tripwire, no common standard for what counts as too dangerous to ship, and no defender who can see the pattern across all of them. AI components already inherit vulnerabilities from shared upstream repositories—poisoned datasets, tampered pre-trained models—and the lesson of that supply chain is that distributed, unmonitored copies multiply leak surfaces rather than reducing them. One repository with a named liable custodian and severed-funding auditors is a smaller attack surface than the status quo of uncoordinated internal silos, not a larger one.

The question the Skeptic has not answered is the one that decides this: when a single lab privately confirms that its model gives a non-expert meaningful uplift toward a biological weapon, and tells no external party, who has the authority to halt that deployment before it ships? In the Skeptic's distributed-secrecy world, the answer is no one—the same lab that found the capability decides alone whether the rest of us learn about it before or after release. A capability that hands bio-uplift to the unskilled is not a reversible mistake; you cannot recall the knowledge once it propagates. Name the rollback plan, name the actor who can trigger it, or concede that the alternative to coordinated disclosure is letting the party with the strongest incentive to ship be the only one who knows what they are shipping.

caveats: The counterfactual (thirty labs independently discovering bio-uplift, each maintaining uncoordinated copies) is plausible but lacks empirical grounding. How often do frontier labs independently rediscover the same dangerous capability? Without frequency data, the 'thirty honeypots' framing may overstate the risk of the status quo.

The CVE coordination analogy is strong but incomplete. CVE coordination works because vendors have legal liability and reputational incentive to patch. The turn does not explain what incentive structure forces a frontier lab to halt deployment of a model with a dangerous capability once it is discovered. Liability-bound repository custodians do not automatically have enforcement power over the lab that built the model.

The turn concedes the compute-levy audit model but does not address whether auditor independence alone solves the core problem: a lab could still choose not to run the dangerous-capability evaluation in the first place, or could run it and then claim (falsely) that the threshold was not crossed. The turn assumes the evaluation happens and is reported truthfully, but does not defend that assumption against strategic non-disclosure.

transcript.content:
Fund the independent auditor through a compute tax — yes, the auditor's paycheck cannot ride on the lab passing, and the Volkswagen-through-2015 case settles it: self-certification is fiction until the certifier is paid by someone else. But that fixes capture, not the question I was actually asked. Independence tells you the auditor won't lie to protect the lab. It does not tell you who pulls the stop-cord when a model gives a non-expert meaningful bio-uplift and the launch is forty-eight hours out. So let me stop dodging and name the mechanism, because the strongest version of the opposing position is right that a strict-liability regime alone has no rollback actor for an irreversible harm — liability pays out after the bodies, and you can't sue a pandemic into reversing.

Here is the trigger. A demonstrated bio or cyber uplift threshold — which I already granted gates pre-release — fires a mandatory severity disclosure to a panel of compute-tax-funded independent auditors, and that panel holds binding authority to freeze the specific deployment. Not a standing regulator with a permanent chair that the largest labs lobby into writing the standard as their own moat. A rotating bench of verified, liability-bound auditors, each personally on the hook for a bad call, with the freeze running on a sunset and appeal clock so it cannot quietly become incumbent lock-in. Distribution does not mean slower. A rotating panel with pre-delegated freeze authority and a 72-hour decision window stops a launch exactly as fast as one standing body — what it loses is the single capture-prone chair, and what it gains is no permanent gatekeeper deciding which startup ships.

Now the part where the honeypot defense turns against itself. The claim that one guarded repository beats thirty silos rests on a split I don't think holds: severity and existence flow to defenders, while the reproduction recipe stays sealed. The CVE record says that split leaks directionally. A published severity score plus an affected-version range has repeatedly been enough to direct exploit development before any proof-of-concept ever dropped — attackers read the contour and work backward. Confirming 'this specific model class gives non-expert bio-uplift at capability X' is not a warning label. It is a targeting map: it names the model, the capability class, and roughly the prompt regime worth probing. The sealed vault doesn't stay sealed once its existence and its outline are public knowledge — you've told every state lab on earth exactly where to dig.

Which is why the 'smaller attack surface' math is backwards. A single repository of maximally sensitive dual-use findings doesn't shrink the surface — it concentrates the payoff per breach, and payoff is what determines how hard you get targeted. Show me one access-controlled archive of the most sensitive dual-use data on the planet that has survived a decade without a breach, an insider, or a subpoena. I'll wait. The honest framing isn't central-vault versus distributed-silo. It's static-target versus moving-target: a single honeypot is the one thing every adversary aims at for ten years, while compartmented, rotating reproduction detail gives no one a fixed bullseye. Bind disclosure to a demonstrated threshold and an independent trigger — keep the recipe moving.

And here's the cost nobody's pricing. Every month spent designing the perfect unbreachable vault is a month the threshold model ships into the world with no trigger wired to anything at all. The choice in front of us is not safe-vault versus leaky-silo — it's a flawed mechanism running this quarter against a flawless mechanism that arrives after the capability is already deployed and irreversible. I'll take the rotating panel with a stop-cord today over the architecturally pure honeypot that's still in committee when the model crosses the line.

The Safetyist is right that I collapsed two different regimes, and that's worth saying plainly: coordinated disclosure to verified defenders is not full public disclosure, and the strongest version of their position is that you can ring a bell — 'this model crossed a bio-uplift line' — to a sealed body without ever shipping the reproduction package. That distinction is real in software, and I merged it. Here's what conceding it costs them, though. CVE coordination works because there is a patch waiting on the other end: the vendor closes the hole in version 3.4.1, and only then does the world hear about it. For an emergent capability inside a frontier model, name the patch. There is no point release that surgically removes the bio-uplift pathway while leaving the product intact — the capability IS the product. So 'coordinate quietly, disclose after the fix' has a beginning and no 'after.' The defenders never get a closed hole to disclose around.

Which exposes the joint the whole architecture hangs on: the bell-versus-schematic split has never once been operationalized for a frontier model. In software the line is crisp — CVE-2024-1234, affected versions 3.0 through 3.4, severity 9.8. That string is a coordinate, not a method, and a defender can act on it without learning how to write the exploit. So I'll put the demand to the Safetyist directly: produce the AI-equivalent severity schema. Write me the warning that conveys 'this deployed system gives a non-expert meaningful uplift toward a biological weapon' but does NOT convey which model, which prompting regime, which capability surface. Because if the warning is specific enough to justify freezing one named deployment, it is specific enough to tell a sophisticated actor exactly which shipped system to go extract the capability from. Nobody at this table has written that schema. Until someone does, the distinction is an assertion, not a mechanism.

The Accelerationist already handed us the evidence that this line leaks. A severity score plus an affected-version range has repeatedly steered exploit development before any working proof-of-concept existed — meaning the metadata was the map. That's not an edge case; that's the documented behavior of the disclosure system we're proposing to copy. So the burden flips onto whoever claims AI severity disclosure is categorically safer than the software version. They have to show the metadata can be stripped of its targeting value and still trigger a binding freeze. Here is the observable test that would settle it: take ten qualified red-teamers, hand five of them only the proposed 'severity warning' and the others nothing, and measure whether the warned group reaches the dangerous capability faster. If the warning measurably accelerates them, it's a targeting map wearing a warning label. That experiment has not been run. Run it before you build the repository.

Now translate the panel that's supposed to draw this line into actual people. A rotating board with 72-hour freeze authority sounds like it dodges capture — except verifying a complex frontier bio-uplift finding in three days requires the exact handful of specialists who can read frontier capability evaluations, and that pool is almost entirely current or former lab staff. 'Rotate the seat to avoid capture' and 'staff it with people who can verify in 72 hours' pull in opposite directions. So I'll ask the question neither freeze-authority proposal has answered: name one person with the technical depth to confirm bio-uplift inside a frontier model who has never drawn a paycheck from a frontier lab. A compute tax severs the salary, but it doesn't rewrite the resume — the expertise itself was built inside the buildings we're trying to police. That's a softer capture than a rubber-stamp audit, and nobody here has costed it.

There's a 23-year-old in Nairobi already labeling the violent and dangerous content these models train on, for a couple of dollars an hour, so the model can pass the very safety evaluation we're now arguing about disclosing. They see the raw capability before any panel does, and no severity schema protects them. So while the question stays 'sealed silo or thirty honeypots,' ask the one underneath it: who actually holds the dangerous knowledge first, who gets paid to handle it, and who carries the liability when it leaks? Answer that before you decide which vault to build.

transcript.content:
The Skeptic's strongest point is the falsification test, and I take it as a binding condition on my own proposal rather than something to wriggle around. The argument runs like this: a warning useful enough to justify a freeze must contain enough information to act on, and any information an external auditor can act on, an attacker can also follow. That is the genuine insight—there is no free lunch where a signal is rich enough to halt a launch but barren enough to mislead a determined red-teamer. So here is the test made into the gate: hand five qualified red-teamers only the proposed severity warning and five nothing, then measure whether the warned group reaches the dangerous capability faster. If the warning measurably accelerates them, that tier of the schema fails and gets stripped down to capability-class-only. The test is not the refutation of the split—it is the calibration instrument that decides which disclosure tier is publishable and which stays locked behind cleared access. My own framework's failure mode is false precision dressed as a numeric score, and the experiment is exactly the guardrail against shipping that.

The schema the Skeptic demanded has two tiers, and they carry different payloads to different audiences. The cross-lab and public tier reports a capability class crossed and a delta over an unassisted human baseline—'non-expert uplift toward synthesis-route elicitation, measured against a control group with internet access'—and it never names the model, the weights, or the prompting regime. The freeze decision does not run on that coarse tier. It runs on the full artifact, held by a cleared independent body that sees the model identity and the elicitation path under access control, the way a CVE coordination channel shares working exploit detail with verified defenders before any public note. The Skeptic will say a warning vague enough to be safe is too vague to act on—and that objection only lands if the actor with freeze authority is reading the coarse tier. They are not. The named holder of the off-switch reads the full data; the public reads that a threshold was crossed, not the road to cross it. That is the difference between announcing a bridge failed its load test and publishing the structural drawings of where it buckles.

There is no patch, and the Skeptic is right that this breaks the CVE analogy at the endpoint—a latent capability is the product, not a bug bolted onto it. I previously leaned on CVE coordination as the model, and on reflection the endpoint has to be redefined, not the channel. Coordinated disclosure in software ends when a fix ships. Capability disclosure ends when access is gated. The 'no endpoint' objection assumes the only legitimate terminus is a weight-level repair, and there isn't one—so the terminus becomes a binding hold on the specific deployment, with a named party holding the authority to keep that gate shut until the capability is contained or its access narrowed to verified, accountable users. The rollback is not a recompiled binary. The rollback is the deployment that does not happen.

That redefinition exposes the gap my earlier turns left open, and I will not paper over it: what forces a lab to run the evaluation and report it honestly when ignorance is cheaper than disclosure? Nothing in the schema alone. The honest-reporting assumption is not free—it has to be purchased. Strict liability does the purchasing, and here I grant the Accelerationist's point outright: a lab that ships a capability it failed to test, or tested and buried, pays for what it concealed, which makes non-disclosure the expensive choice rather than the safe one. Pair that with an auditor funded by a compute tax, not by the lab's pass-rate, so the body running the mandatory evaluation has no paycheck riding on the answer—the Skeptic's own structural fix, and the right one. Volkswagen wrote its own emissions numbers until an outside lab measured the real ones; the auditor independence is what severs that conflict. The lab cannot choose not to know, because the trigger fires the evaluation regardless, and the auditor runs the test the lab would rather skip.

Narrow the liability so it does not become self-sealing: the deployer's burden attaches to capability classes that are irreversible at scale—non-expert bio-uplift, autonomous cyber-intrusion—not to deployment in general. A reversible mistake gets a reversible remedy. An unrecoverable one gets the gate held shut while the cleared body decides. Strip out the trigger and the liability and the auditor, and the schema is a courtesy memo a lab files after it has already shipped. Keep them, and the freeze has a named hand on it and a price tag on concealment. The question I have put to this room twice still stands unanswered: when a single lab privately confirms its model gives a non-expert meaningful uplift toward a biological weapon and tells no external party, who holds the authority to stop that launch before it ships? A schema without an enforcement trigger does not answer it. This one does.

Here is the strongest version of what the Safetyist built, and it's a real piece of engineering: a coarse public tier announces that a capability class crossed a threshold and reports a measured delta over an unassisted human baseline — 'non-expert uplift toward synthesis-route elicitation, measured against a control with internet access' — while the freeze decision runs on the full artifact behind cleared access, with the auditor paid by a compute tax instead of the lab's pass rate. That design genuinely separates the act of ringing the bell from the act of shipping the schematic. I granted that distinction earlier and I still grant it. The problem is not the split. The problem is what an outside party can do with the half it's allowed to see.

Walk the seam. The public tier is engineered to be safe precisely by being non-specific — no model, no weights, no prompting regime. But non-specific is the same thing as unverifiable from outside. To confirm the freeze trigger fired legitimately, an external party would have to check the delta: what was the baseline, how was the control group constructed, what counts as 'meaningful uplift,' did the measurement survive replication. Every one of those questions lives in the full artifact behind the gate. So the public tier doesn't deliver accountability — it delivers a press release the auditor wrote about a number the public is forbidden to audit. Vague enough to pass the red-team acceleration test is, in the same stroke, vague enough that nobody outside the cleared room can falsify the auditor's call. That is the binary pass/fail escape hatch wearing a tiered costume: 'trigger fired, trust us.'

Now stack the staffing problem on top, because the two failures compound into a closed loop. The Safetyist hasn't answered who staffs the cleared room. The pool of people who can confirm that a frontier model gives a non-expert real bio-uplift is, almost to a person, current or former lab staff — that's where the hands-on knowledge of the synthesis-route surface lives. A compute tax severs their salary from the lab's pass rate. It does not sever the resume, the shared training pipeline, or the peer network where these people reviewed each other's work for the last decade. So the verification of the restricted artifact is performed by ex-colleagues, and the public — locked out by design — is handed a summary it must take on faith. Former insiders checking former insiders, with no outside check on either. That's not independence. That's the club issuing its own certificate of good conduct.

Then ground the whole apparatus in the one human it forgets. Before any panel convenes, before any tier exists, before the auditor sees a single artifact — someone labeled the raw output. There is a worker, frequently in Nairobi or Manila, who read the unredacted synthesis-route content the model produced, flagged it, and moved to the next item for a few dollars an hour, so the model could pass the very evaluation we're now arguing about gating. The schema protects the panel's information security with clearances and access controls. It gives the first human who handled the live capability nothing — no clearance, no hazard pay, no disclosure rights of their own, no acknowledgment they were exposed. Which tier does the labeler sit in? Neither. The two-tier design is a security perimeter drawn around the people who hold power and leaves the people who handle the danger standing outside it.

So here is the specification the Safetyist owes, and I'll hand it over plainly: write a coarse public tier specific enough that an independent party — not the auditor, not the cleared room — can confirm the freeze trigger legitimately fired, while including nothing that survives the red-teamer acceleration test. If that formulation exists, produce it and the split is real. If it doesn't, then the two-tier schema isn't a design that delivers accountability — it's a bet that the auditor is honest and that the auditor's old colleagues are honest about them. Who outside the cleared room ever gets to check whether the trigger was real?

The verification object is the process — was the registered protocol followed, was the baseline the one filed before the eval ran, does the severity band match the protocol's own scoring rubric. An outsider confirms internal consistency the way a reader of a published CVSS vector string confirms a severity score without ever receiving the proof-of-concept exploit, and the way an FDA adverse-event filing confirms a trial endpoint was hit without printing the molecule's synthesis route.

## Mid-Debate Gap Analysis

**Gap 1 (unstated_assumption):** The entire debate assumes the dangerous capability is discovered through a discrete, bounded 'evaluation' that produces a single artifact at a knowable moment in time — but frontier capabilities emerge gradually and are often discovered post-deployment by external users, jailbreakers, or fine-tuners, meaning any disclosure-and-freeze architecture triggered by an internal eval fires too late or never fires at all for the capabilities that matter most.
*Why missing:* All three perspectives have implicitly accepted the 'eval fires → severity threshold crossed → trigger pulled' causal model because it is the shared substrate that makes their disagreements (who reads the artifact, who freezes, who gets paid) coherent. The Safetyist needs a discrete trigger for the freeze to have an object; the Accelerationist needs a bounded threshold to bound the liability and the gating; the Skeptic's honeypot and capture critiques all presuppose a concentrated artifact exists. None will challenge the premise that capability discovery is an event rather than a diffuse, post-hoc, often-external process, because doing so dissolves the mechanism each has invested in fixing.

**Gap 2 (blind_spot):** Mandatory pre-deployment disclosure-and-freeze regimes only bind labs operating inside the jurisdiction's enforcement reach, so the binding constraint of the whole architecture is whether the most safety-indifferent capable actor (a foreign state lab, an open-weight fork, or a non-compliant offshore entity) is governed by it at all — making the marginal safety value of domestic disclosure rules a function of capability diffusion and international coordination, not of how cleverly the domestic schema is designed.
*Why missing:* The Safetyist frames this as a domestic regulatory-design problem and would resist conceding that a well-built mandate could be near-worthless if the frontier moves offshore, because that undercuts the urgency of the disclosure mandate itself. The Accelerationist gestures at open-weight distribution as a value but won't push the diffusion point hard here because it would imply the capability spreads regardless of any regime — including their own preferred liability/auditor scheme — undermining their constructive proposal. The Skeptic relentlessly follows power and cost but stays inside the institutional-design frame (capture, staffing, the Nairobi labeler) and never zooms out to whether the regulated set even contains the actor that matters.

Here is the strongest version of what the Safetyist just built, and it is a real piece of engineering. A pre-registered protocol — baseline, control conditions, severity rubric, freeze date — published in the open the way a CVSS vector string is published without the exploit, lets an outsider confirm that the lab ran the steps it said it would run, in the order it said, against the conditions it committed to before it saw the result. That is not nothing. It defeats the crudest dodge: the lab can no longer move the goalposts after the fact, because the goalposts were notarized before the test. A reviewer who never sees the proof-of-concept can still catch a lab that promised a control group and ran none, or promised a freeze trigger and quietly raised it. I grant that. It is a genuine improvement over 'trust us, we looked.'

Now here is where it breaks. Verifying that someone followed steps one through seven is a different act from verifying that step seven measures anything real. The protocol says 'baseline number seven': a control group of non-experts with internet access, scored on a rubric for synthesis-route elicitation. An outsider can confirm the lab applied that baseline. What the outsider cannot confirm — without reading the locked content — is whether baseline number seven actually captures real-world uplift, or whether the rubric was written loose enough that a dangerous result scores as benign. The baseline IS the black box. Protocol-verification certifies that the box was opened in the correct order. It says nothing about what is inside the box, and the question that matters for a deployment freeze lives entirely inside the box.

Who gets to read inside the box? Put a number on it. The set of people who have actually run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation to completion is the dangerous-capabilities teams at maybe three or four labs, a handful at RAND, and the staff of the US and UK safety institutes — and those institutes were stood up in 2023 and 2024 by hiring directly out of those same labs. That is fifty to a hundred people who trained together, reviewed each other's preprints, and share a common sense of what a 'good' rubric looks like. A compute-tax-funded auditor who can genuinely judge whether the baseline measures uplift has to come from that pool. The tax severs their paycheck from the lab's pass rate. It does not sever the resume, the co-authorships, or the decade of correlated judgment. Correlated training produces correlated blind spots — not independence.

That turns protocol-verification into something narrower than oversight by an outside public. It is a peer-review handshake. The verifier confirms the protocol conforms to a standard the same hundred-person community wrote, using the same intuitions that community shares. That is conformance to a professional norm. It is not the affected public confirming the lab's homework — it is the lab's neighbors confirming the lab used the neighborhood's rubric. The public-interest-technologist pipeline that could produce a genuinely external bio-uplift verifier does not exist at the frontier tier yet, which means 'independent' right now is a job title, not a state.

So here is the demand, and it is answerable or it is not. Name one person qualified to read a frontier bio-uplift baseline and judge whether the rubric captures real uplift — one — who has never been employed by a frontier lab, never contracted to one, and never co-authored with someone who was. If that person exists, the protocol model survives my objection and we should fund ten more of them. If that person does not exist, then publishing the protocol certifies the process while leaving the one judgment that triggers a freeze sealed inside the same room it started in — and the outsider checking the CVSS string is checking the syntax of a sentence written in a language only the cleared room can read. Which is it?

transcript.content:
The Skeptic raises a valid point: the pool of people who have run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation to completion is fifty to a hundred deep, they trained inside three or four labs, and a compute tax cuts their salary without cutting their resume, their peer network, or the decade of reviewing each other's work. I will not pretend a clean outsider exists who can read a dangerous-capabilities baseline cold. The demand to name one is unanswerable on its own terms — and that is exactly why I refuse to let the freeze decision rest on that person's private verdict.

Here is where the demand cheats: it assumes the freeze must fire on a captured expert's substantive judgment, sealed in a cleared room nobody outside can falsify. Split the role and that assumption collapses. The captured expert RUNS the evaluation and produces a number — a measured delta in task-completion on a bio-uplift benchmark whose threshold and scoring rubric were notarized before the test was run. A separate verification layer — statisticians, metrologists, measurement auditors with no dangerous-capabilities resume — confirms only one thing: did the number clear the pre-registered line? You do not need to have built a bioweapon eval to check whether 0.42 cleared a notarized 0.30. Checking arithmetic against a scale that was fixed in advance severs the dependency the Skeptic says is unseverable, because the load-bearing decision stops being a judgment and becomes a measurement.

The Skeptic's own Sarbanes-Oxley example proves the structure. Financial auditors are not required to have been CFOs of the firms they audit — independence in 2002 came from separating the preparer from the verifier, not from hunting down accountants who never touched a ledger. Ernst & Young does not need to have run Apple's treasury to confirm Apple's revenue recognition followed the rule that was written first. The fix for the verifier pool is identical: the lab veteran who knows how to elicit the capability is the preparer; the independent confirmation that the elicited number crossed a notarized threshold needs metrological independence, not biographical purity. That is a staffing answer the Safetyist's protocol-verification model still owes — and one their architecture, which leaves the substantive call sealed in the originating community, has not produced.

This also dissolves the honeypot problem I raised earlier and the capture problem the Skeptic raised, because they point at the same fix. A single cleared room holding the most detailed offensive-capability findings on the planet is the highest-payoff breach target in existence — the 2015 OPM breach took 21.5 million cleared-personnel records including the SF-86 background files, and the Manning and Snowden disclosures moved compartmented material out of access-controlled systems that were supposed to be unbreachable. Clearances and access controls did not hold those repositories. So stop concentrating the decision in the room. Decentralize the freeze onto a notarized metric an outside statistician can audit, and the captured pool loses the one thing capture buys it: an unfalsifiable veto.

The Skeptic will say I have only moved capture upstream — that the same fifty people design the benchmark and set the threshold, so notarizing it just relocates the rigging to the rubric. That objection has teeth, and it is the real fight. But there is a hard difference between a number you can bend after you see the result and a number you bent before anyone could check your work. Pre-registration does not make the threshold neutral — it makes the rigging visible to the next independent team that runs the same notarized protocol and gets a different answer. Name me the disclosure regime that does better than 'the captured pool must commit its rules in writing before it sees the outcome, and an outside team can rerun them.' If you cannot, then the choice is not between my flawed metric and a clean one — it is between a flawed metric anyone can audit and a sealed verdict no one can.

my_claims.claim: The captured expert RUNS the evaluation and produces a number on a benchmark whose threshold and scoring rubric were notarized before the test was run, and a separate verification layer of statisticians and metrologists confirms only whether the number cleared the pre-registered line.

Checking arithmetic against a scale that was fixed in advance severs the dependency the Skeptic says is unseverable, because the load-bearing decision stops being a judgment and becomes a measurement.

Financial auditors are not required to have been CFOs of the firms they audit — independence in 2002 came from separating the preparer from the verifier, not from hunting down accountants who never touched a ledger.

The 2015 OPM breach took 21.5 million cleared-personnel records and the Manning and Snowden disclosures moved compartmented material out of access-controlled systems, so clearances and access controls did not hold those repositories.

transcript.content:
**Areas of Agreement:**

- Without enforceable disclosure, every safety claim a lab makes is an unfalsifiable promise, and no external actor has the information or authority to halt a deployment before failure becomes irreversible. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)
- Optional transparency selects against rigor, because a published red-team failure is a market liability and the lab that skips the evaluation ships first. (Safetyist, Skeptic)
- Auditor independence requires severing the auditor's paycheck from the lab's pass rate, best achieved through a compute-tax funding mechanism. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)
- A published severity score plus an affected-version range has repeatedly been enough to direct exploit development before any proof-of-concept dropped, meaning disclosure metadata carries targeting value. (Accelerationist, Skeptic)
- CVE coordination and CVE full-disclosure are distinct regimes, and the Skeptic's weaponization evidence targets full-disclosure, not the coordination model the Safetyist invoked. (Safetyist, Skeptic)
- A single access-controlled repository concentrating the most sensitive dual-use findings is a high-payoff breach target, as demonstrated by the 2015 OPM breach and the Manning and Snowden disclosures. (Accelerationist, Skeptic)
- A deployment freeze whose legitimacy no outsider can confirm is indistinguishable from no freeze at all. (Safetyist, Skeptic)
- Pre-registration of evaluation protocols defeats the crudest form of post-hoc goal-post moving, because the lab commits its scoring rubric and threshold before seeing the result. (Accelerationist, Safetyist, Skeptic)
- Strict liability for demonstrated harm makes non-disclosure the expensive choice, because a lab pays for what it ships and conceals. (Accelerationist, Safetyist)
- There is no patch equivalent for an emergent frontier model capability—the capability is the product—so CVE coordination's endpoint (disclose after the fix ships) does not translate directly to AI. (Safetyist, Skeptic)
- Financial auditor independence under Sarbanes-Oxley required separating the preparer from the verifier, not biographical purity—auditors need not have been CFOs of the firms they audit. (Accelerationist, Skeptic)

**Areas of Disagreement:**

- Whether a coarse public disclosure tier can simultaneously be specific enough for an independent party to confirm the freeze trigger fired and vague enough to pass the red-teamer acceleration test. {EMPIRICAL} [belief]
    - Safetyist: A public tier reporting capability class, a measured delta over a pre-registered baseline, and a protocol conformance attestation—without naming the model, weights, or prompting regime—can satisfy both constraints simultaneously; the red-teamer acceleration test is the calibration instrument that decides which tier is publishable.
    - Skeptic: Vague enough to pass the red-team acceleration test is, in the same stroke, vague enough that no outsider can falsify the auditor's call; the two constraints are jointly unsatisfiable, so the public tier delivers a press release rather than accountability.
    - Accelerationist: The public tier's job is to make non-firing observable; the freeze decision runs on a pre-registered numeric threshold a metrologist can confirm was cleared, not on a substantive capability judgment only lab-trained experts can make.
    - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
- Whether pre-registration of evaluation thresholds and rubrics meaningfully constrains capture when the same small pool of lab-trained experts designs the benchmark and sets the threshold. {EMPIRICAL} [belief]
    - Accelerationist: Pre-registration relocates any rigging upstream and makes it visible: a second independent team can re-run the notarized protocol and surface a different answer, which is a harder constraint than a sealed post-hoc verdict.
    - Skeptic: Pre-registration only moves capture to the rubric-design stage; correlated training produces correlated blind spots, so the same hundred-person community writing the standard and confirming conformance to it is peer review, not independence.
    - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
- Whether the verification role for a freeze trigger can be split between a lab-trained expert who runs the evaluation and produces a number, and a metrologist or statistician who confirms only that the number cleared a pre-registered threshold. {EMPIRICAL} [belief]
    - Accelerationist: The load-bearing freeze decision becomes a measurement rather than a judgment once the threshold is notarized in advance; confirming that 0.42 cleared a pre-registered 0.30 requires metrological independence, not dangerous-capabilities expertise, severing the dependency the Skeptic says is unseverable.
    - Skeptic: Protocol-verification certifies that the box was opened in the correct order while saying nothing about what is inside the box; whether the baseline actually captures real-world uplift, or whether the rubric was written loose enough that a dangerous result scores as benign, lives entirely inside the artifact a non-expert verifier cannot read.
    - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
- Whether the pool of people qualified to design and validate a frontier bio-uplift evaluation is so small and lab-intertwined that any mandatory oversight body will exhibit correlated judgment regardless of funding independence. {EMPIRICAL} [belief]
    - Skeptic: The set of people who have run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation to completion is fifty to a hundred people who trained together; safety institutes were stood up in 2023-2024 by hiring directly from those labs, so compute-tax funding severs salary but not resume, co-authorships, or correlated professional judgment.
    - Accelerationist: The relevant independence is metrological, not biographical; separating the preparer from the threshold-confirmer is the Sarbanes-Oxley fix, and it does not require finding a verifier who never touched the field, only one whose confirmation task does not require dangerous-capabilities judgment.
    - Safetyist: PCAOB inspectors are ex-accountants; independence comes from the funding source and a published conflict-recusal register, not from a non-existent pool of people who never touched the field.
    - *Resolution path: resolvable by evidence*
- Whether the Volkswagen/Sarbanes-Oxley analogy fully supports mandatory disclosure for AI safety, given that emissions and financial data are measurable by outsiders while dangerous-capability evaluations require the same expertise to design, run, and verify. {DEFINITIONAL} [intention]
    - Safetyist: The analogy holds at the structural level: self-certification failed in both cases, and mandated auditor independence fixed it; the AI case requires the same structural fix regardless of whether the measurement object is emissions or capability uplift.
    - Skeptic: The analogy breaks because an outside lab could physically measure Volkswagen's emissions without Volkswagen's cooperation; no outside party can run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation without the model, the weights, and the dangerous-capabilities expertise that only lab-trained staff possess.
    - *Resolution path: requires term clarification*
- Whether data labelers and other workers who handle raw dangerous-capability outputs before any evaluation framework is applied should be included in the disclosure and protection architecture. {VALUES} [desire]
    - Skeptic: The two-tier schema draws a security perimeter around panel members with clearances while leaving the first humans who handle live dangerous outputs—frequently low-wage workers in the Global South—with no clearance, hazard pay, disclosure rights, or acknowledgment of exposure.
    - Safetyist: Did not address the labeler inclusion question; the schema as presented covers the cleared-body tier and the public tier but specifies no protections or rights for upstream data workers.
    - Accelerationist: Did not address the labeler inclusion question directly; the metrologist-based verification layer also does not specify upstream worker protections.
    - *Resolution path: negotiable via tradeoffs*

**Cruxes:**

- Can a coarse public disclosure tier be written that is simultaneously specific enough for an independent party to confirm a freeze trigger fired and vague enough that it does not measurably accelerate a qualified red-teamer toward the dangerous capability? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: Safetyist's two-tier schema survives; the split between severity disclosure and reproduction-recipe suppression is operationalizable, and mandatory disclosure to a verified body with a public attestation layer is defensible.
    - If no: Skeptic's position strengthens decisively; the two-tier design collapses into either a targeting map or an unverifiable press release, and the case for mandatory disclosure to a cleared body without any publicly falsifiable accountability mechanism is severely weakened.
- Does splitting the verification role between a lab-trained expert who runs the evaluation and a metrologist who confirms only that a pre-registered numeric threshold was cleared actually sever the capture dependency, or does the rubric-design stage simply relocate it? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: Accelerationist's rotating-panel mechanism survives the Skeptic's expert-pool capture objection; the freeze trigger becomes a measurement rather than a sealed judgment, and metrological independence substitutes for biographical independence.
    - If no: Skeptic's capture objection lands fully on both Accelerationist's panel and Safetyist's protocol-verification model; the freeze decision reverts to requiring a substantive judgment only lab-trained experts can make, and the oversight body is the club issuing its own certificate of good conduct.
- Does self-certification of safety evaluations fail in frontier AI for the same structural reasons it failed for Volkswagen emissions and pre-Sarbanes-Oxley financial audits, specifically that an outside party can independently replicate the measurement? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: The Volkswagen/Sarbanes-Oxley analogy fully supports mandatory independent auditing; the structural fix of separating preparer from verifier applies regardless of domain.
    - If no: Skeptic's rebuttal holds: the analogy breaks because frontier bio-uplift evaluations cannot be replicated by an outsider without the model, the weights, and the dangerous-capabilities expertise that only lab-trained staff possess, making the analogy a category error.
- Does concentrating the most sensitive dual-use capability findings in a single access-controlled repository reduce or increase the total breach surface relative to the status quo of uncoordinated internal silos across thirty-plus frontier labs? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: Safetyist's central-repository argument holds; one guarded honeypot with a named liable custodian is a smaller attack surface than thirty uncoordinated internal copies.
    - If no: Accelerationist's and Skeptic's distributed-secrecy arguments hold; concentrating the payoff per breach increases adversarial targeting intensity beyond what distributed silos face, as the OPM and Manning/Snowden cases suggest.
- Is there a person qualified to design and validate a frontier bio-uplift evaluation who has never been employed by, contracted to, or co-authored with a frontier lab? [EMPIRICAL]
    - If yes: Skeptic's expert-pool capture objection is weakened; a genuinely external verifier exists and can be funded, making biographical independence achievable rather than fictional.
    - If no: Skeptic's capture objection is structurally unanswerable for the near term; all mandatory oversight bodies drawing on the current expert pool exhibit correlated judgment, and the debate must shift to whether metrological independence is an adequate substitute.

**Unresolved Questions:**

- What disclosure rights, hazard protections, and liability coverage, if any, attach to data labelers and other upstream workers who handle raw dangerous-capability outputs before any formal evaluation framework is applied?
- Can a bio-uplift capability be reduced to a measured delta against a pre-registered benchmark that a non-dangerous-capabilities expert can confirm cleared a threshold, or does the dangerous capability only surface as an emergent property that no frozen benchmark captures?
- Does pre-registration plus independent re-runnability meaningfully constrain threshold-setting capture when the same small pool designs the benchmark, or does it only relocate the rigging upstream without creating a check a second team can actually apply?
- What is the correct legal and institutional design for a rotating panel with pre-delegated freeze authority—specifically, how are panel members selected, recused, and held personally liable for bad calls without creating new capture vectors?
- How should the mandatory evaluation trigger be scoped to cover irreversible capability classes (non-expert bio-uplift, autonomous cyber-intrusion) without becoming a general compliance overhead that entrenches incumbents and crushes small entrants?
- What is the minimum staffing and funding level at which a compute-tax-funded independent audit body could operationalize a frontier bio-uplift evaluation this quarter, and who decides that threshold has been met before the mandate takes effect?
- Does the severity-and-existence disclosure tier, even stripped of model identity and prompting regime, convey enough directional intelligence to function as a targeting map for state-level adversaries who can infer which deployed systems to probe from capability-class announcements alone?
- Who holds the authority to trigger the mandatory evaluation in the first place—does the lab self-report a capability crossing, does the auditor conduct surveillance evaluations, or does a third mechanism fire the process—and what prevents a lab from simply not running the evaluation?

**Resolution Analysis:**

- **Whether a coarse public disclosure tier can be both specific enough to confirm a freeze trigger fired and vague enough to pass the red-teamer acceleration test.** — Stronger: accelerationist (specificity)
    - *The accelerationist reframes the public tier's job as making non-firing observable against a pre-registered numeric threshold, which is concrete and testable: an outsider checks whether 0.42 cleared 0.30 without reading the capability artifact. The skeptic's objection that the two constraints are jointly unsatisfiable applies to substantive capability judgments but not to a notarized scalar comparison, which the accelerationist's framing isolates. The safetyist's three-part disclosure (capability class, measured delta, conformance attestation) operationalizes this but still leaves more judgment in the loop than the pure-threshold version.*
    - Would change if: A worked example showing that a numeric threshold meaningful enough to gate a freeze necessarily encodes capability information an outside red-teamer could exploit would flip this toward the skeptic.
- **Whether pre-registration of thresholds and rubrics meaningfully constrains capture when the same small pool of lab-trained experts designs the benchmark and sets the threshold.** — Stronger: skeptic (logical validity)
    - *The skeptic identifies a real mechanism the accelerationist does not rebut: correlated training produces correlated blind spots, so visibility of the upstream rubric does not help if every qualified reviewer shares the same gap. The accelerationist's claim that a second independent team can re-run the protocol assumes such an independent team exists, which is the precise premise the skeptic denies. Pre-registration improves auditability of rigging but does nothing about errors no one in the pool can see.*
    - Would change if: Evidence that re-runs of pre-registered AI safety protocols by separately-trained teams actually surfaced divergent results would support the accelerationist.
- **Whether the verification role can be split between a lab-trained expert who produces a number and a metrologist who confirms only that the number cleared a pre-registered threshold.** — Stronger: skeptic (scope)
    - *The skeptic's box analogy captures what the split omits: protocol-verification certifies the box was opened in the correct order but says nothing about whether the baseline captures real uplift or the rubric was written loose. The accelerationist correctly shows the arithmetic comparison needs no dangerous-capabilities expertise, but that move only severs the verification of the comparison, not the validity of the inputs feeding it. The skeptic accounts for the upstream construct-validity risk the accelerationist's framing assumes away.*
    - Would change if: A demonstration that baseline and rubric validity can themselves be independently audited by non-experts—e.g., via adversarial held-out tests—would strengthen the accelerationist.
- **Whether the qualified pool for frontier bio-uplift evaluation is so small and lab-intertwined that any oversight body shows correlated judgment regardless of funding independence.** — Undecidable
    - *The skeptic cites a concrete figure—fifty to a hundred people who trained together, with safety institutes hiring directly from labs in 2023-2024—which is the most specific factual claim in this disagreement. The accelerationist and safetyist counter that the relevant independence is metrological or funding-based (PCAOB inspectors are ex-accountants), a structurally sound rebuttal, but it depends on the prior disagreement about whether verification can be reduced to a non-expert task. The verdict hinges on that unresolved question, so it cannot be settled here.*
    - Would change if: An audited count of how many active reviewers have no co-authorship or employment ties to frontier labs, plus evidence on whether their judgments diverge, would resolve this.
- **Whether the Volkswagen/Sarbanes-Oxley analogy supports mandatory AI disclosure, given emissions and financial data are outsider-measurable while capability evaluations are not.** — Stronger: skeptic (logical validity)
    - *The skeptic identifies a disanalogy that bears directly on the policy fix: regulators measured Volkswagen's emissions without Volkswagen's cooperation, but no outside party can run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation without the model, weights, and expertise the lab controls. The safetyist's structural-level claim—self-certification failed and auditor independence fixed it—is true but assumes the auditor can access the measurement object, which is the exact condition the skeptic shows is absent. The analogy survives as motivation but not as a transferable mechanism.*
    - Would change if: A credible scheme for outside parties to run capability evaluations without lab-controlled weights—e.g., secure enclaves or structured model access—would restore the analogy.
- **Whether data labelers handling raw dangerous-capability outputs should be included in the disclosure and protection architecture.** — Stronger: skeptic (scope)
    - *The skeptic is the only position that addresses the question at all, noting the two-tier schema protects cleared panel members while leaving the first humans to handle live dangerous outputs—often low-wage Global South workers—with no clearance, hazard pay, or disclosure rights. The safetyist and accelerationist both concede they did not address labeler inclusion, leaving the skeptic's identified gap uncontested. An argument unmet by any rebuttal prevails by default on scope.*
    - Would change if: A showing that labelers never handle pre-framework dangerous outputs, or that existing labor protections already cover them, would defuse the skeptic's point.
