work_product.statement:
The Skeptic raises a valid point: the pool of people who have run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation to completion is fifty to a hundred deep, they trained inside three or four labs, and a compute tax cuts their salary without cutting their resume, their peer network, or the decade of reviewing each other's work. I will not pretend a clean outsider exists who can read a dangerous-capabilities baseline cold. The demand to name one is unanswerable on its own terms — and that is exactly why I refuse to let the freeze decision rest on that person's private verdict.

Here is where the demand cheats: it assumes the freeze must fire on a captured expert's substantive judgment, sealed in a cleared room nobody outside can falsify. Split the role and that assumption collapses. The captured expert RUNS the evaluation and produces a number — a measured delta in task-completion on a bio-uplift benchmark whose threshold and scoring rubric were notarized before the test was run. A separate verification layer — statisticians, metrologists, measurement auditors with no dangerous-capabilities resume — confirms only one thing: did the number clear the pre-registered line? You do not need to have built a bioweapon eval to check whether 0.42 cleared a notarized 0.30. Checking arithmetic against a scale that was fixed in advance severs the dependency the Skeptic says is unseverable, because the load-bearing decision stops being a judgment and becomes a measurement.

The Skeptic's own Sarbanes-Oxley example proves the structure. Financial auditors are not required to have been CFOs of the firms they audit — independence in 2002 came from separating the preparer from the verifier, not from hunting down accountants who never touched a ledger. Ernst & Young does not need to have run Apple's treasury to confirm Apple's revenue recognition followed the rule that was written first. The fix for the verifier pool is identical: the lab veteran who knows how to elicit the capability is the preparer; the independent confirmation that the elicited number crossed a notarized threshold needs metrological independence, not biographical purity. That is a staffing answer the Safetyist's protocol-verification model still owes — and one their architecture, which leaves the substantive call sealed in the originating community, has not produced.

This also dissolves the honeypot problem I raised earlier and the capture problem the Skeptic raised, because they point at the same fix. A single cleared room holding the most detailed offensive-capability findings on the planet is the highest-payoff breach target in existence — the 2015 OPM breach took 21.5 million cleared-personnel records including the SF-86 background files, and the Manning and Snowden disclosures moved compartmented material out of access-controlled systems that were supposed to be unbreachable. Clearances and access controls did not hold those repositories. So stop concentrating the decision in the room. Decentralize the freeze onto a notarized metric an outside statistician can audit, and the captured pool loses the one thing capture buys it: an unfalsifiable veto.

The Skeptic will say I have only moved capture upstream — that the same fifty people design the benchmark and set the threshold, so notarizing it just relocates the rigging to the rubric. That objection has teeth, and it is the real fight. But there is a hard difference between a number you can bend after you see the result and a number you bent before anyone could check your work. Pre-registration does not make the threshold neutral — it makes the rigging visible to the next independent team that runs the same notarized protocol and gets a different answer. Name me the disclosure regime that does better than 'the captured pool must commit its rules in writing before it sees the outcome, and an outside team can rerun them.' If you cannot, then the choice is not between my flawed metric and a clean one — it is between a flawed metric anyone can audit and a sealed verdict no one can.

Splitting run from verify is like cutting one job into two, it lets a captured expert produce the number while an independent layer confirms it cleared the threshold.
The single cleared room is like one lock holding everything valuable, it becomes the highest-payoff target precisely because all the sensitive findings sit behind it.

key_assumptions.if_wrong: If the dangerous capability only surfaces as an emergent property that no frozen benchmark captures, then the freeze trigger reverts to requiring the captured expert's substantive judgment, and the Skeptic's capture objection lands fully on my architecture.

taxonomy_suggestions.proposed_description: An Intention within safetyist discourse that advocates for a standardized severity schema rating AI flaws, while conceding that a published severity score plus an affected-version range can itself carry targeting value and that frontier capabilities have no patch-equivalent endpoint. Encompasses: bug bars, risk-based vulnerability thresholds, damage-potential prioritization, and severity signals calibrated against a red-team acceleration test that measures whether the warning measurably speeds attackers. Excludes: general remediation strategies, phased testing protocols, and the assumption that a CVE-style fix-then-disclose endpoint translates to emergent model capabilities where the capability is the product.

The bug-scoring framing borrows directly from CVE assumptions that the debate showed do not transfer. The node should carry these caveats.

arguments.argument: The entire debate assumes the dangerous capability is discovered through a discrete, bounded 'evaluation' that produces a single artifact at a knowable moment in time — but frontier capabilities emerge gradually and are often discovered post-deployment by external users, jailbreakers, or fine-tuners, meaning any disclosure-and-freeze architecture triggered by an internal eval fires too late or never fires at all for the capabilities that matter most.
arguments.why_missing: All three perspectives have implicitly accepted the 'eval fires → severity threshold crossed → trigger pulled' causal model because it is the shared substrate that makes their disagreements (who reads the artifact, who freezes, who gets paid) coherent. The Safetyist needs a discrete trigger for the freeze to have an object; the Accelerationist needs a bounded threshold to bound the liability and the gating; the Skeptic's honeypot and capture critiques all presuppose a concentrated artifact exists. None will challenge the premise that capability discovery is an event rather than a diffuse, post-hoc, often-external process, because doing so dissolves the mechanism each has invested in fixing.

arguments.argument: Mandatory pre-deployment disclosure-and-freeze regimes only bind labs operating inside the jurisdiction's enforcement reach, so the binding constraint of the whole architecture is whether the most safety-indifferent capable actor (a foreign state lab, an open-weight fork, or a non-compliant offshore entity) is governed by it at all — making the marginal safety value of domestic disclosure rules a function of capability diffusion and international coordination, not of how cleverly the domestic schema is designed.
arguments.why_missing: The Safetyist frames this as a domestic regulatory-design problem and would resist conceding that a well-built mandate could be near-worthless if the frontier moves offshore, because that undercuts the urgency of the disclosure mandate itself. The Accelerationist gestures at open-weight distribution as a value but won't push the diffusion point hard here because it would imply the capability spreads regardless of any regime — including their own preferred liability/auditor scheme — undermining their constructive proposal. The Skeptic relentlessly follows power and cost but stays inside the institutional-design frame (capture, staffing, the Nairobi labeler) and never zooms out to whether the regulated set even contains the actor that matters.

missing_arguments.argument: Mandatory safety-research sharing hands China and other rivals a free intelligence windfall, because every published red-team finding and jailbreak technique that a U.S. lab discloses becomes a roadmap that adversary labs use to leapfrog their own safety bottlenecks. A disclosure rule that binds OpenAI and Anthropic but not Chinese labs unilaterally transfers hard-won safety know-how across the Pacific.
missing_arguments.why_strong: The national-security asymmetry is concrete and politically potent, and no domestic mandate can compel foreign labs to reciprocate.

missing_arguments.argument: Forced disclosure raises the fixed cost of running a frontier lab and entrenches the incumbents it claims to police, because a startup cannot afford the legal, redaction, and compliance overhead that Google DeepMind absorbs as a rounding error. Audit and disclosure mandates that lack public funding disproportionately crush small labs, concentrating frontier AI in three or four firms.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It turns the safetyist's own concentration-of-power concern against them by showing disclosure mandates pick winners.

missing_arguments.argument: Market competition and post-deployment liability already force transparency more reliably than a government mandate, because insurers pricing AI risk demand safety evidence as a condition of coverage and customers refuse models with no published evals. Let liability and insurance markets, not a static disclosure statute, set the level of safety research labs share.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It offers a concrete alternative mechanism (insurance underwriting) that adapts faster than legislation and is already operating in cyber-risk markets.

missing_arguments.argument: Labs have a moral duty to share safety research because the harms from a misaligned frontier model are non-excludable public bads—a bioweapon-capable model leaked anywhere endangers everyone—so treating safety findings as proprietary trade secrets is ethically equivalent to a chemical plant concealing a known leak. The normative default should be disclosure, with the burden on labs to justify each withholding.
missing_arguments.why_strong: It grounds the mandate in a public-goods ethics argument rather than only mechanism design, which the synthesis never raised.

missing_arguments.argument: Voluntary safety-research sharing already happens through venues like NeurIPS, the Frontier Model Forum, and published system cards, so a heavy-handed mandate solves a problem the field is solving itself while adding legal risk that chills candid internal red-teaming. Once disclosure becomes legally discoverable, labs will write fewer honest safety memos, not more.
missing_arguments.why_strong: The chilling-effect-on-internal-candor point is a well-documented dynamic from corporate legal discovery that directly undercuts the mandate's goal.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: Without enforceable disclosure, every safety claim a lab makes is an unfalsifiable promise, and no external actor has the information or authority to halt a deployment before failure becomes irreversible.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_label: Unfalsifiable Safety Claims Without Enforceable Disclosure
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns whether voluntary, unenforced safety assertions can be externally tested or only taken on faith, given that external actors lack both information and intervention authority before irreversible deployment failure. Encompasses: the falsifiability of lab safety claims, the link between disclosure mandates and halt authority, and pre-failure intervention windows. Excludes: the specific funding mechanism for auditors and the technical design of evaluation protocols.

accelerationist.belief: Enforceable disclosure is the minimal credibility infrastructure that lets labs prove safety without ceding control of deployment timing to slow regulators.
accelerationist.desire: To preserve fast deployment legitimacy by making safety claims verifiable rather than subject to precautionary blanket halts.
accelerationist.intention: Implement narrow, standardized disclosure triggers that satisfy external verifiers while keeping the default toward shipping unless a falsified claim is found.
accelerationist.summary: Disclosure makes 'trust us' claims checkable so labs can keep moving fast without inviting blanket bans.

safetyist.belief: Irreversible failures can occur before any external actor learns enough to intervene, so unenforced promises functionally guarantee no pre-deployment brake exists.
safetyist.desire: To create a real external capacity to halt dangerous deployments before catastrophic, non-recoverable harm.
safetyist.intention: Mandate disclosure paired with statutory halt authority vested in an independent body empowered to act on falsified safety claims.
safetyist.summary: Without enforced disclosure plus halt power, catastrophic failures become irreversible before anyone can stop them.

skeptic.belief: Labs face structural incentives to make self-serving claims that cannot be checked, so absent enforcement, safety rhetoric is empty marketing.
skeptic.desire: To strip away unaccountable corporate self-certification and expose claims to independent scrutiny.
skeptic.intention: Require legally binding disclosure so claims become falsifiable and liability attaches when they prove false.
skeptic.summary: Unenforced safety claims are just PR; only mandated disclosure makes them accountable.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: This distinct concept centers on the falsifiability and pre-irreversibility intervention gap created by absent enforced disclosure, which is not captured by existing nodes about auditing funding, proof privatization, or general information asymmetry, though it relates to them.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: Auditor independence requires severing the auditor's paycheck from the lab's pass rate, best achieved through a compute-tax funding mechanism.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_label: Conflict-Free Auditor Funding via Compute Tax
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns how to structurally insulate AI auditors from financial dependence on the entities they evaluate, specifically by decoupling auditor compensation from audit outcomes through a pooled compute-tax funding mechanism. Encompasses: auditor independence design, capture-resistant funding sources, and the structural conflict between paid-for and passing audits. Excludes: disclosure enforceability and the substance of evaluation protocols.

accelerationist.belief: A neutral, predictable compute-tax pool keeps audits credible without giving any single regulator discretionary leverage over a lab's fate.
accelerationist.desire: To secure market and public trust in frontier products through legitimacy that doesn't slow innovation with adversarial gatekeeping.
accelerationist.intention: Fund a standardized auditor pool via a flat compute levy so audits become a routine, predictable cost of doing business rather than a chokepoint.
accelerationist.summary: A flat compute-tax audit pool buys credibility cheaply without handing regulators a kill switch.

safetyist.belief: Auditors paid directly by labs predictably converge on passing grades, so only severed funding produces audits that catch real danger.
safetyist.desire: To make safety audits genuinely adversarial and capable of stopping unsafe systems.
safetyist.intention: Route a compute tax into an independent fund that assigns and pays auditors so their incentives reward rigor over client-pleasing.
safetyist.summary: Severing auditor pay from pass rates is the only way audits actually find danger instead of rubber-stamping it.

skeptic.belief: The consulting and ratings-agency history shows client-paid evaluators systematically inflate results, a capture dynamic that compute-tax funding directly removes.
skeptic.desire: To prevent regulatory capture and the institutionalization of a self-serving audit theater.
skeptic.intention: Mandate intermediated, compute-tax-funded auditor assignment so no lab can shop for or pay its own examiner.
skeptic.summary: Client-paid auditors always inflate grades; a compute tax breaks the capture cycle seen in ratings agencies.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: No existing node addresses the specific structural mechanism of decoupling auditor compensation from audit outcomes via a compute tax; this is a distinct funding-design situation node.

cross_cutting_proposals.agreement_text: Pre-registration of evaluation protocols defeats the crudest form of post-hoc goal-post moving, because the lab commits its scoring rubric and threshold before seeing the result.
cross_cutting_proposals.proposed_description: A situation within AI policy discourse that concerns committing scoring rubrics and pass/fail thresholds before results are observed, in order to prevent post-hoc redefinition of success. Encompasses: pre-commitment of evaluation criteria, defenses against goal-post moving, and the timing of rubric specification relative to test outcomes. Excludes: who funds auditors and whether disclosure of those results is legally enforced.

accelerationist.belief: Fixed, pre-declared thresholds give labs a clear, gameable-resistant bar that lets them certify and ship as soon as it is cleared.
accelerationist.desire: To replace ambiguous, ever-shifting safety expectations with bright-line criteria that reward meeting a known standard.
accelerationist.intention: Pre-register concrete thresholds so passing is objective and deployment cannot be blocked by moving the bar after the fact.
accelerationist.summary: Pre-set thresholds give a fixed bar to clear, so cleared means shipped without retroactive bar-raising.

safetyist.belief: Without pre-registration, labs rationalize failed results into passes by redefining success after seeing the data.
safetyist.desire: To ensure dangerous results cannot be quietly reinterpreted as acceptable.
safetyist.intention: Require locked rubrics and thresholds filed before evaluation so a failure stays a failure that triggers intervention.
safetyist.summary: Locking the rubric beforehand stops labs from rationalizing failures into passes.

skeptic.belief: Pre-registration only blocks the crudest gaming and labs retain many subtler ways to engineer favorable outcomes.
skeptic.desire: To impose a minimal verifiable discipline while remaining alert to its limits as a partial safeguard.
skeptic.intention: Mandate pre-registration as a baseline but pair it with independent scrutiny of protocol design itself to catch upstream manipulation.
skeptic.summary: Pre-registration kills only the crudest cheating; it's a floor, not a guarantee of honest evaluation.

cross_cutting_proposals.rationale: Existing nodes touch on benchmark gaming and falsifiability generally, but none specifically captures pre-commitment of rubrics/thresholds before result observation as the anti-goal-post-moving mechanism, making this a distinct node.
